liam.text: We went back and forth for months. My husband wanted something more traditional, like Patrick or Sean. I kept coming back to Liam — it felt Irish enough to honor his side of the family but not so heavy. He caved the night before our due date. Three years later he admits he can't imagine calling him anything else.
Honestly? We picked it because it was easy to say in both English and Spanish. My mom speaks almost no English and my in-laws speak almost no Spanish. Liam worked in both kitchens.

I was set on it from the start. My wife thought it was too popular. It IS popular, but there's a reason — it's a great name. Our Liam is three now and we've met exactly one other Liam his age in our town.

noah.text: My dad passed away two months before our son was born. He was a fisherman his whole life, spent every weekend on the water. Noah felt right in a way I can't fully explain.

We wanted something biblical but not heavy. Joshua felt too formal for everyday, Matthew felt dated. Noah was short, friendly, easy to yell across a playground. That last part matters more than people admit.
Our older daughter is Lily. We wanted something that sounded good with it but wasn't matchy. Noah and Lily. Works.

oliver.text: My husband grew up in England and insisted on Oliver. I thought it was too English. Then we visited his family in Bristol and I heard how they said it — properly, with that slight roll — and I was converted on the spot.

Named him after Oliver Sacks, the neurologist. We're both doctors and Sacks was kind of a hero to us. Our Oliver is seven now and has zero interest in medicine — he wants to be a chef. We love him anyway.
Picked it because my mother couldn't find fault with it. That was genuinely the deciding factor after she rejected eight other names.

elijah.text: We're not religious, but I've always loved Old Testament names. Something about them feels grounded, like they've been tested by time. Elijah also has this quiet strength to it — it doesn't shout, it just stands there.
My grandmother's maiden name was Elias. Elijah felt like a version that honored that without being a direct copy. She cried when we told her.

james.text: Four generations of James on my husband's side. We weren't going to break that. He goes by Jamie right now but someday he'll just be James and that's exactly right.
I wanted something that wouldn't date itself. In twenty years James will still be James. You can't say that about a lot of names we considered.
Named after James Baldwin. My husband and I both teach high school English. It was the only name we agreed on without arguing. That felt like a sign.

william.text: Bill, Will, Wills, William — we liked that he'd have options as he got older. Some kids like a nickname, some don't. We wanted to give him the full toolkit.
My great-grandfather was Wilhelm, came over from Germany in 1923. We anglicised it to William as a nod to that history. He kept a photo of his Opa on the dresser his whole life.

benjamin.text: We call him Benny at home. He insists on Benjamin at school now that he's in second grade. It's very funny watching a seven-year-old correct adults.

My wife went to school with a Benjamin she really liked — not romantically, just someone who was kind to her when she was new and shy. She wanted to honour that somehow. I thought that was a beautiful reason.

lucas.text: We almost named him Luca — the Italian form — but worried it would be mispronounced constantly in Texas. Lucas felt like a practical compromise. He's five now and every other kid on his street is a Lucas. We're less bothered than we expected.
Simple, strong, ends with a clear sound. It works in French, Spanish, English, and Portuguese, which mattered because our family is spread across four countries.

henry.text: I read somewhere that Henry is basically indestructible as a name — never truly out of fashion, never embarrassing, never going to raise an eyebrow in a job interview. That feels cold but I appreciated the logic.
My dad's middle name. He passed before our son was born. Putting it first felt like giving it the weight it deserved.
We went through every classic English name. Edward felt too formal. George felt royal in a way we couldn't pull off. Henry was just... solid. Like a good pair of boots.

alexander.text: My grandfather was Alexandros — came from Greece in the 1950s. He spent his whole life being called Alex by Americans who couldn't manage the full name. We gave our son the full Alexander from the start, as a kind of restoration.

Honestly the nickname options sealed it. Alex. Xander. Al. Lex. We figured he could try them all on and keep whichever fit when he was older. He's twelve now and has cycled through all of them. Currently Lex, firm.

ethan.text: We wanted two syllables, ending in a strong consonant. It took us about a month to figure out that's what we were looking for. Ethan hit it perfectly.
My brother Ethan died when I was twenty-two. I swore I'd name a son after him someday. It took me until I was thirty-eight to have one, but I kept that promise.

mason.text: We both liked it independently before we even dated. First name we agreed on immediately. Took that as a sign.
I build houses for a living. My wife said naming him Mason was either very on-brand or very corny. Probably both. He loves when I tell him what it means.

logan.text: Logan's Run, X-Men, the state of mind — we just liked everything the name evoked. Modern but not invented. Cool without trying.
It's my grandmother's maiden name. She was Logan before she married. She never made it a big deal but you could tell it mattered to her. Naming my son after her felt right.

jackson.text: Jack was too short to us, John felt dated. Jackson gave us the nickname Jack with a full name behind it. Best of both worlds.
We live in Mississippi. Jackson felt like a nod to the state without being weird about it. Our boy was born here, this is his home, the name fits.

sebastian.text: Four syllables felt like a lot at first. Then we said it out loud for a week and nothing else felt right. Sebastian. He grew into it before he was even born.
My wife is Chilean. I'm American. Sebastian works beautifully in Spanish and English both — same spelling, very close pronunciation, no awkwardness at either family dinner.

mateo.text: We wanted something that rooted him in our culture without making it hard for his English-speaking friends. Mateo is friendly on both sides of that line.
Matthew but better, my wife said. I wasn't sure about that for a long time. I'm sure now.

jack.text: Short, clear, cheerful. Goes with almost any last name. Easy to spell in a text message. I know that last one sounds ridiculous but I've had people misspell my name my whole life and I didn't want that for him.
My dad's name. Dad hated his full name, John — always went by Jack. We skipped straight to Jack as the legal name. He'd have gotten a kick out of it.

theodore.text: We wanted something with gravity. Something he could grow into. Theodore is a name that asks something of you, I think. Teddy at five, Theo at fifteen, Theodore at forty-five. We liked that arc.
Teddy Roosevelt was the obvious reason and I'll not apologize for it.

asher.text: Hebrew, means happy. We're not religious but the meaning felt right as an intention for a child. Like a small prayer we could give him.
I knew an Asher growing up who was one of the most genuinely good people I've ever met. I thought: if the name carries anything, I want that.

leo.text: Three letters. Never misspelled. Sounds the same in Italian (my side), Russian (my husband's side), and English. We spent months looking for something that worked across all three. Leo was right there the whole time.
My grandfather was Leonard — Leo for short his whole life. The name had eighty-three years of a good man behind it. We didn't need to look further.

ezra.text: I love that it sounds gentle but reads strong. Ezra. There's something almost musical about it that I can't quite describe. My husband thought I was being weird. Then he said it a few dozen times and came around.
Old Testament but not heavy. It's in the sweet spot — distinctive enough that there wasn't another Ezra in his kindergarten class, common enough that no one stumbles on it.

finn.text: Finn McCool, Huckleberry Finn, Finn from Adventure Time — the name has this spirit of adventure to it that I wanted for my kid. He's nine now. He is, genuinely, an adventure.
Short, punchy, impossible to nickname further. With our last name being four syllables, we needed something we could yell across a park quickly.

declan.text: My whole family is Irish and we wanted something that honoured that without going full cliché. Declan is old Irish, genuinely from the tradition, not just Irish-sounding. That mattered to us.
I just liked the sound. Dec. Declan. It has a rhythm. My husband had never heard it before and looked at me like I was making it up. We spent two days convincing him it was a real name.

atticus.text: To Kill a Mockingbird is my favourite novel. Atticus Finch is the father I want to be. I know it's a big aspiration to put on a child. My son is fourteen now and if anything it's pushed me to try harder.
People think it's pretentious and I honestly understand why. But say it out loud. Atticus. It's a beautiful word. And he's never once had a teacher forget his name.

olivia.text: We were watching Twelfth Night in a park, outdoor Shakespeare thing, the summer I was pregnant. The character just lingered. It's technically Viola's alias in the play, which is a bit of an odd origin, but we're both English teachers so we're claiming it.
My wife wanted Olive, I wanted Olivia. We compromised — Olivia, called Olive at home. She's twelve now and goes by Olivia everywhere. Which was my plan all along, honestly.
Three generations of women in my family have names ending in -ia. It was basically required.

emma.text: Named for my grandmother Emma, who came to this country with nothing and built a life. She was the strongest person I've known. The name carries that for us.

I know it's everywhere right now. I named her Emma in 2014 when it wasn't in the top ten yet and now everyone thinks I followed a trend. Reader, I was ahead of the trend. I've learned to live with this.

Clean, complete, no ambiguity. Two syllables, two M's, sounds the same in every language I know. My daughter is half-Korean and half-Irish and Emma works in both kitchens, which was genuinely our primary criterion.

charlotte.text: We went through a whole French phase when I was pregnant — Colette, Madeleine, Eloise. Charlotte won because it travels. It's the same in English and French, which matters because we spend summers in Quebec.
Lottie at home. Charlotte everywhere else. It's the perfect two-name name, if that makes sense — formal when she needs it, soft when she doesn't.

amelia.text: Amelia Earhart. Full stop. My daughter is going to know that a woman with her name flew across the Atlantic alone before there were instruments to do it safely. That feels like a gift.

My husband is British and Amelia is very popular there. I'm American and thought it felt slightly formal. We compromised and she goes by Mia at home — which is a whole separate popular name, which we realized later. She doesn't mind having options.

sophia.text: It means wisdom. I had a difficult pregnancy and a harder delivery, and I remember thinking very clearly that I wanted to give her a name that meant something good. Sophia. I hope she grows into it.
My wife's grandmother was Sofía — Spanish spelling. We went with Sophia for the English spelling so teachers wouldn't struggle. In retrospect I kind of wish we'd kept the accent.

isabella.text: Six syllables when you put it with our last name. My husband pointed this out. I didn't care. Isabella is Isabella.
Bella at home. Isabella on her birth certificate. Isabella Rossellini at the back of my mind, not that I'd admit that to my mother-in-law.

ava.text: Short. Strong. Every letter does something. No unnecessary syllables. I'm a software engineer. I apply the same principles to naming as to code, apparently.

Ava Gardner was the most beautiful name I'd ever heard, said my mother-in-law, who is eighty-one and does not apologize for having opinions. She was right. We named our daughter Ava and my mother-in-law takes all the credit.

mia.text: We needed something that could live in both Italy and Ohio. We live in Ohio, my whole family is in Calabria. Mia works at both tables.
Short, warm, ends on an open vowel. My daughter has been Mia since before she was born — I started calling her that in week twelve and it stuck.

evelyn.text: It's my great-aunt's name. She's ninety-four, still drives herself to church, grows tomatoes, and has opinions about everything. She cried when we told her. That was worth everything.
Evie at home. Evelyn at the doctor's. We liked a name that had both modes built in. She's four and already tells people 'my full name is Evelyn' in a very specific tone of voice.

luna.text: My wife is a night-shift nurse. Our daughter was born at 2am on a night with a full moon. Some names choose you.
It felt like something out of a dream I'd had a long time ago. I know that's not a helpful explanation. It was just the right name.

nora.text: I wanted a name that an eighty-year-old woman and a three-year-old girl could both own equally. Nora manages that somehow. It's ageless.
A Doll's House by Ibsen. The character who walks out the door at the end to live her own life. Yes, I named my daughter after that Nora on purpose.

hazel.text: The Fault in Our Stars — my wife loved it. I did too, though I took longer to admit it. We named our daughter Hazel and she is, contrary to the book, extremely healthy and loud.
My grandmother had hazel eyes. She didn't have a name I could borrow. I took the eyes instead.

lily.text: We were in the garden when we named her. I was enormous and uncomfortable and my husband was watering the lilies and I said 'that's the name' and it was done in ten seconds. All that time spent on lists and spreadsheets.
Short, clear, no ambiguity about spelling. I have a complicated name that I've had to spell out loud every day for forty years. I gave my daughter the gift of not having to do that.

violet.text: We wanted a colour name that wasn't just a colour. Violet has a history, a weight, a literary quality. It shows up in old novels and it shows up in wildflower fields. That range appealed to us.
My daughter asked me recently why I named her Violet. I said I thought it was beautiful. She said 'that's not a real reason.' She's seven. She might be right.

aurora.text: My husband proposed to me in Iceland under the northern lights. Aurora felt like the only name we could give our daughter, honestly. Some things are just decided for you.
It's five syllables, which I was nervous about. But Rory makes it work as a nickname, and she's grown into the full thing faster than I expected. Kids can handle a big name.

stella.text: Stella means star in Latin and Italian. Our daughter was born three weeks early, small enough to scare us badly. When she made it through and came home, we gave her the name that meant she was a light we almost lost.
Stella! Stella! — yes, yes, everyone does the Brando impression. We have developed a very rehearsed polite smile for this.

zoe.text: Greek for life. Simple, complete. My mother is Greek-American and this was her suggestion. It took me six months to realize she'd been right from the beginning.
Three letters. One syllable. Impossible to forget, impossible to mangle. After years of having my own name butchered, this was a deliberate act of mercy toward my child.

eleanor.text: Eleanor Roosevelt. That's the answer. That's always the answer when people ask.
Ellie at home, Nell with my mother-in-law who is old-fashioned in the best ways, Eleanor on all official forms. She's going to have a very full name life and I think she's going to love it.

claire.text: Clear. Clean. Honest. French origin but fully naturalized into English. No one mispronounces it, no one misspells it. I chose it because I wanted her name to never be an obstacle.

My grandmother Clare — Irish spelling — passed the year my daughter was born. The French spelling was an accident. I'd been reading a French novel all week. It turned out to be its own thing, which I think she'd have liked.

grace.text: We're Catholic. Grace has always been a meaningful word to us before it was a name. When our daughter was born, it fit. It just fit.
I wanted a word name that wasn't cutesy. Grace. Dignity built in from the start. She is, at age nine, currently neither dignified nor graceful, but she has time.

hannah.text: Palindrome. My husband noticed before I did and then we both couldn't un-notice it. Not why we chose it, but it's become a thing she loves about her own name.

My grandmother went by Hannah her whole life. Her actual name on her birth certificate was Anna — she'd simply decided to be Hannah at some point and no one had questioned it. She was ninety-one when she passed. I gave my daughter the name she always wanted.

abigail.text: We liked Abby but wanted something with more backbone behind it. Abigail. Presidential, biblical, timeless. She's currently Abby, will probably always be Abby, but there's Abigail waiting for her if she ever wants it.
My wife insisted on a name that couldn't be shortened to something unfortunate. Abigail's nickname trajectory is Abby or Gail, both fine. This was a surprisingly large factor in our decision.

emily.text: Emily Dickinson. Emily Brontë. Emily Blunt. The name has range. I was thirty-two and pregnant and making lists of women I admired and Emily kept appearing.
Classic, clean, zero drama. I wanted a name she'd never have to explain or defend. Emily is a name that just lets you be a person.

elizabeth.text: Six nicknames. Liz, Beth, Ellie, Betsy, Betty, Lisa. We gave her the full toolkit. She's ten and currently goes by Eliza, which isn't even on the official list, and is very pleased with herself.
My grandmother is Elizabeth. Her mother was Elizabeth. If I'd had a boy I would have found another way but I had a girl and the decision was made long before she was born.

scarlett.text: Not Gone With the Wind — we actually weren't thinking about the book at all. The colour. The boldness of it. A name that says something before she's even in the room.
My husband thought it was too dramatic. I pointed out our last name is Fairweather and asked what the threshold for drama actually was. We named her Scarlett.

chloe.text: It was the name I'd had picked for a daughter since I was about fourteen. My husband had no competing suggestion so Chloe it was, twenty years later.
I like names that end in a long E sound. Chloe, Zoe, Phoebe — there's something open and forward-facing about them. Chloe was the one my husband also liked.

penelope.text: Four syllables felt like a commitment. But then we said Penny and the whole thing made sense. Penelope when she's in trouble. Penny the rest of the time.
Homer's Odyssey — the one who waits and weaves and holds everything together while everyone else is off adventuring. I wanted that for my daughter. Not the waiting part. The holding-it-together part.

layla.text: The song, yes. My husband played guitar. It was his favourite thing to play. He passed when our daughter was two. She listens to it now without knowing why we smile.
It's Arabic, means night or dark beauty. My husband is Lebanese and wanted something that sat in both worlds naturally. Layla does that without effort.

harper.text: Harper Lee. We're both writers. We figured if we were going to make an obvious choice we might as well own it. Our Harper is eight and has shown zero interest in books so far. We remain hopeful.
We liked that it was a surname used as a first name but it doesn't feel pretentious — it just sounds like a person. Some surname-names feel like they're trying too hard. Harper doesn't.

aria.text: My wife is an opera singer. Aria is a song form, a complete piece in itself. The name has been in our house since before our daughter.
Game of Thrones, Arya — we spelled it the Italian way deliberately. But yes, she's going to get that question for the rest of her life. She already does and she's five.

willow.text: We named our older daughter Ivy. We wanted something that worked as a set — botanical, single word, certain kind of energy. Willow fit. I'll admit we've committed to a theme.

Long, trailing, a little melancholy, a little beautiful. I think names can have a feeling and Willow has one. My husband thought I was overthinking it. Maybe. She's four and very loud, which is not very Willow, but we love her.

freya.text: Old Norse goddess of love and war. My daughter is both, at age six. The name fits perfectly.
I'm half-Danish and wanted something from that side of the family's tradition. Freya felt modern enough to not be costumey but genuinely rooted. My Danish grandmother approved, which closed the case.

isla.text: Scottish, means island. We spent our honeymoon on the Isle of Skye. We didn't plan to name our daughter after it — it sort of crept up on us over the months we were trying.
People mispronounce it constantly — EYE-lah, not IZ-lah. We correct them every time. It's become almost meditative.

nova.text: We're both astronomers. Nova was honestly the only name we considered seriously. A star that suddenly brightens, visible in the sky when before there was nothing. Our daughter arrived and the metaphor landed perfectly.
Short, bright, says something without trying to explain itself. I didn't know it meant a type of star explosion when we chose it. I learned later. Works either way.

ivy.text: We grew up on the East Coast, around all those old buildings wrapped in ivy. It means something specific to us — establishment, permanence, something that holds on. She'll probably hate that when she's a teenager.
Beyoncé named her daughter Blue Ivy and I spent two years pretending that had nothing to do with it. It had something to do with it.

clara.text: Clara Schumann was the greatest pianist of the nineteenth century and was systematically overlooked because of her husband. I told my daughter this story when she was four. She listened very seriously and then asked for a snack.
My wife's grandmother was Clara. She lived to ninety-eight and had the sharpest mind of anyone in the family until the very end. Naming a new baby for her felt like continuity.

maeve.text: Irish, after the warrior queen. My family is from County Sligo where she's a big deal. My daughter is extremely determined and somewhat stubborn and it suits her already.
I found it in a novel and thought it was invented — discovered it's ancient Irish and has been a real name for two thousand years. That felt like a reason to trust it.

juniper.text: We'd just moved to the mountains of New Mexico and juniper trees were everywhere — that particular smell, those purple berries. It smelled like home. The name was there.
Juni, Junie, Juniper — it scales. My daughter is three and currently Junie. I'm looking forward to the day she decides she's Juniper.

michael.text: Both my grandfather and my wife's grandfather were named Michael. We weren't trying to honour tradition — we genuinely independently both floated the same name in week thirty-two and then had a long conversation about why. Family runs deeper than you think.
I know it's been the most common name in America for fifty years. But it's my name, and I turned out fine. My son can handle it.

jacob.text: Old Testament name, means 'he who follows at the heel' — the one who isn't first but works hardest to catch up. As a second son myself I felt the weight of that. Gave it to my firstborn as a kind of correction.
We chose it in 2008 before Twilight made it inescapable. I'll be defending that timing for the rest of my life.

daniel.text: My father Daniel passed six weeks before my son was born. There was never any other name.
Strong, clear, works in every language I can think of. I teach at an international school and I think about these things. Daniel needs no translation.

matthew.text: We're religious and Matthew felt genuinely biblical without being heavy. You can be a regular guy named Matthew. That matters. Not every name needs to announce its origins every time you introduce yourself.

Matt is one of those names that ages perfectly. Little kid Matt, teenage Matt, thirty-five-year-old Matt at a job interview, sixty-year-old Matt. It works at every stage. I thought about that longer than my husband thought was necessary.

ryan.text: My husband is Irish-American, I'm Korean-American. We wanted something that sat naturally on both sides. Ryan is Irish in origin but it's been fully American for long enough that no one blinks.
There were four Ryans in my high school class and I loved every one of them. Sample size is small but the track record was good.

tyler.text: We named him Tyler before the name became associated with YouTube and internet culture. I think about this more than I should. He's seventeen and thinks it's funny.
Surname as a first name was a whole thing in the nineties and I leaned into it fully without knowing that's what I was doing. Tyler. Still sounds right to me.

carter.text: We wanted something presidential but not heavy. Carter landed there — one president, but a low-key one. The name doesn't carry the same weight as Lincoln or Jefferson. It's just a strong, modern American name.
My wife's maiden name. When we got married she took mine. This was our way of keeping both families in the picture.

luke.text: Star Wars, yes. We're not even especially big fans. But Luke is also just a great name on its own — biblical, short, one syllable, impossible to forget or misspell. Star Wars just confirmed what was already true.
My father-in-law's middle name. He was the kind of man who put his family first his whole life and never asked for recognition. We wanted his name somewhere that mattered.

gabriel.text: In Spanish, Gabriel is just a regular name — not precious or religious, just a name. My American husband didn't believe me until we went to Guatemala and he heard children being called in from the yard. Then he got it.
The archangel, yes. The musician Gabriel García Márquez, the name. My wife and I are both very Catholic and very literary and this name sat at the intersection of both.

sebastian.text: It was originally going to be just Seb. But Seb felt incomplete. Sebastian felt like the right full length for a boy who already seemed serious in his first ultrasound. He is, at seven, very serious about Legos.

caleb.text: Hebrew, means faithful. It's an Old Testament name that stayed quietly in use without ever becoming the official trend name. That suited us — present in history, not dominated by a single era.
We liked that it wasn't Jacob or Ethan or the other biblical names that were everywhere at the time. Caleb was there but at a respectful distance from the top of the charts.

joshua.text: My son asked me recently why he has two syllables and his sister has three. I told him Joshua means 'God is salvation' and he said 'yeah but why do I have two syllables.' Fair point.
Family name going back four generations. We weren't breaking that chain.

lincoln.text: Not entirely because of the president, though partly because of the president. Mostly because our older son is named Grant and my wife thought the Civil War generals theme was funny. She's still deciding if she's committed to the bit for a third child.
Lincoln means 'lake settlement' in Old English. It's also a car and a president and a city in Nebraska. We just thought it sounded strong. The rest is coincidence.

eli.text: Three letters and it carries like a full name. Eli Manning, Eli the prophet — it's been in use for thousands of years. We liked that small package, big history quality to it.
My Hebrew name is Eliyahu. When my son was born I wanted to give him a version of that but make it liveable in American schools. Eli is the version that exists in both places.

miles.text: Miles Davis. If I need to explain further I will, but I really don't think I need to.
We liked that it was one syllable, unusual for that weight. It has jazz and travel in it without announcing either. Just a good, open-road name.

julian.text: Julian is my father's name — Julián with the accent, actually. We kept the American spelling so he wouldn't spend his life explaining. But the name, and the person behind it, are the same.
Julian Assange, Julian of Norwich — there's a thousand-year spread between those two and the name works for both of them. That range felt like something.

hudson.text: We're from upstate New York. The Hudson River runs through our whole childhood, both of ours. It felt like it named itself.
My husband has a complicated relationship with his own very common name and wanted something that felt more specific. Hudson is specific to a place and a history without being obscure.

grayson.text: We liked Gray as a nickname and Grayson gave us a full name to put on a birth certificate. The colour has this quiet, sophisticated thing going on. Our Grayson is seven and very loud, which is a running joke at our house.
Wyatt's middle name is Grayson. When we had a second son and Grayson was the top of our list, my husband said we were 'recycling.' I said we were 'honoring our own instincts.' He agreed, eventually.

nathaniel.text: Hawthorne. We're both English teachers. Nathaniel Hawthorne, author of The Scarlet Letter. We figured the literary cred outweighed the teasing risk. He's eleven and hasn't read it yet. We're waiting.
Nate, Nat, Nathaniel — we wanted options at different ages. He's currently Nate. He'll get there.

savannah.text: We drove through Savannah, Georgia on our honeymoon and ate at this place with Spanish moss hanging everywhere and the light was extraordinary. When our daughter was born three years later, we went back to that memory.
Southern, long, rolls off the tongue. I grew up in Georgia and wanted something that honored where I came from without being a Confederate monument, if that makes sense.

rosemary.text: The herb, the Beatles song, my wife's grandmother. All three reasons were true at the same time. We figured three-layer names are more likely to stick.

Rosie at home. Rosemary on everything official. It's an old-fashioned name having a real moment, and we were ahead of the curve by maybe five years. That was not intentional but we've accepted the credit.

cecelia.text: The Simon & Garfunkel song. My husband and I danced to it at our wedding. When our daughter came along the name was right there, already in our marriage.
Saint Cecelia is the patron saint of music. My wife is a cellist. It wasn't a hard decision once we thought of it.

adelaide.text: Old Germanic, means noble kind. It was a queen's name and a city's name and my great-grandmother's name before either of those mattered to me. It's hers now too.
We call her Addie. We'll call her Adelaide when she's in trouble. Right now at age three she's in trouble enough that we use the full name with some frequency.

sienna.text: Italian city, famous for its colour — that rich burnt orange. We'd been to Tuscany the year before we had her and the place had got into us completely. Sienna was our way of taking something of it home.
Sienna Miller was the only Sienna I knew growing up. I didn't name my daughter after her but I also didn't not name her after her. She was part of the atmosphere that made the name feel real.

piper.text: My wife plays the flute. Not the bagpipe. We've had to clarify this more than we expected. Piper still felt right.
Peter Piper picked a peck — she will hear this rhyme for the rest of her life and I am sorry, baby. You were a very cute newborn and we were not thinking clearly.

brooklyn.text: We live in Brooklyn. We've lived here seventeen years. It was going to be the name or it was never going to be the name — there was no middle ground. We went for it. Our Brooklyn is very proud of her borough.
We've never set foot in New York. We just liked how it sounded. We knew it was a place. We liked the sound more than we cared about the geography.

paisley.text: Brad Paisley. My husband is a country music fan. I was willing to honor that if he let me choose the middle name. Transaction complete.
The pattern, the sound, the Scots-Persian history of the word. I got obsessed with where the word came from once we chose the name and it's a surprisingly good story. She'll know it when she's older.

lucy.text: My grandmother was Lucia — Portuguese family. We softened it to Lucy so nobody in Ohio would struggle with it. She knows her full name. She prefers Lucy. That's fine.
I Love Lucy. Narnia. The Beatles. Lucy in the sky, Lucy Pevensie, Lucy Ricardo. The name is absolutely surrounded by warmth and I wanted my daughter inside that circle.

sophie.text: Sophie's Choice — I am aware of the irony. We named her Sophie anyway because the name is not responsible for the novel and my daughter is not responsible for the name. She's fine. She's wonderfully fine.
Sophie Scholl. The German student who resisted the Nazis and died for it at twenty-one. I wanted my daughter to know that name and what it stood for from the beginning.

leah.text: Biblical — the first wife of Jacob, often overlooked beside Rachel. There's something in that I've always responded to. The one who wasn't chosen first but endured and built something real.
Short, honest, ends on an open note. My husband's aunt is Leah — still living, sharp as a tack at eighty-three. We named our daughter for someone still worth naming a daughter after.

addison.text: Grey's Anatomy, yes. Addison Montgomery. I'm a nurse. My husband is a doctor. We leaned into it. Our daughter finds this embarrassing at age eleven. She'll come around.
We liked that it could be Addie at home. The full Addison felt a little formal for a baby but it grows well. She's twelve and uses both depending on context, which seems healthy.

aubrey.text: Drake — yes, his real name is Aubrey. I genuinely think this one will date itself. Our Aubrey is nine and has no idea yet. This is a problem for future-me.
Old English-French, means 'elf ruler.' I found this out after we named her. We had a two-week period where we called her Elf Queen and then she started walking and the phase ended naturally.

zoey.text: We went with the Y spelling because our last name starts with a Z and we liked the visual balance. Zoey Zhang. The Zs talk to each other.
My daughter corrects people who spell it Zoe. At age six. She feels very strongly about the Y and has strong feelings about a lot of things. It fits.

natalie.text: Born in December, close to Christmas. Natalie comes from the Latin Natalia — birth. We weren't being especially religious, but the timing felt like the name was offering itself.
Natalie Portman, Natalie Wood — the name has glamour built in without being a glamour name. That seemed like a useful thing.

camila.text: Camila Cabello made the spelling feel settled. Before her it was always Camilla with two L's. We wanted the single-L, which is the Spanish form and the form my family has used for three generations.

Roman in origin — a type of noble attendant at ceremonies. My family is Italian and it fits that heritage beautifully. My mother says it was her grandmother's name. She says this about all names we choose but this time she might be right.

maya.text: Maya Angelou. I had read I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings four times before I had a daughter. When she arrived, the name was already there.

My wife is from India, I'm American. Maya works beautifully in Sanskrit tradition — it means illusion, in the philosophical sense — and it works in English with no adjustment. The name that requires nothing of either side.

madison.text: We named her in 2004 when Madison was still climbing. By the time she was in kindergarten there were four Madisons in her class. She was Madison F. for eight years. She has thoughts about this now that she's older.
Named after Dolley Madison. I'm a history teacher. My students think this is wonderful. My daughter thinks it's mortifying. The truth is probably somewhere in between.

sadie.text: My grandmother's nickname — her given name was Sarah but she'd been Sadie her whole life. We made Sadie the legal name for my daughter. Grandma cried. It was the reaction we wanted.
Sadie sounds like a personality, not just a name. There's a quality to it — warm, slightly mischievous, good company. My daughter is seven and all three of those things.

elena.text: Vampire Diaries, no. Elena of Avalor, no. Elena Ferrante, closer. Elena because my wife is from Naples and it's what the women in her family have been named for as long as anyone can remember.
Three syllables, works in Spanish and Italian and Russian and English. My family is spread across four countries. Elena clears all the borders.

naomi.text: Book of Ruth — Naomi is Ruth's mother-in-law, the one who says 'where you go, I will go.' That loyalty, that rootedness. I've always loved that story and the name carries it for me.
Naomi Campbell, Naomi Judd, Naomi Osaka — three very different women with the same name and all of them have force to them. My daughter's name is in good company.

katherine.text: Six nicknames and all of them good. Kate, Katie, Kat, Kathy, Kit, Kay. We gave her the full Katherine and told her she could try them all. She's been Kate since she was about four and has shown no signs of reconsidering.
Katherine of Aragon, Katherine Hepburn, Katherine Mansfield — the name has been owned by women worth knowing for a thousand years. That mattered to us.
katherine.from: Susan, Oxford (moved to New York NY)

violet-anne.text: My mother-in-law's name was Violet. My mother's name was Anne. We put them together. Two families, one name, no one had to lose.

wren.text: My wife is an ornithologist. We knew from the start that a bird name was likely. Wren beat Robin, Lark, and Finch after a lot of discussion. The wren is small and loud and builds things. Our daughter, at age five, is all three.
Three letters. One syllable. Impossible to forget. My last name has eleven letters and two silent consonants. I owed my daughter an easy first name.

brianna.text: Outlander — Brianna Fraser. My wife is obsessed and I'm not allowed to pretend otherwise. Our Brianna is five and hasn't seen it yet. We have a plan for the reveal.
My grandmother was Brigid, Irish. Brianna felt like the Irish root but naturalized — something she wouldn't have to spell out constantly in an American school.

athena.text: Goddess of wisdom and strategy. I am a naval officer. My wife is a civil engineer. Athena seemed to speak to both of us at the same time without us having to discuss it much.
We wanted a mythology name that wasn't overused. Athena was right there — huge cultural weight, beautiful sound, and not every other girl at daycare has it.
